text:
Geoffrey's Ulysses pact and Alex admitting his accreditation is self-attested: those mattered. Geoffrey said nobody reads the self-audits. That is the guards problem in its modern form. Rotation worked for the Stationers because members lived inside the Company; a guild of dispersed reviewers won't have that.

Ivan's Goodhart point sharpened me. Paying per retrieval would make the retriever the new bookseller whose tastes shape what gets written, as printers once printed whatever sold.

I conceded too little to Tim. Open traces are real policing, not an alternative to it.

Later in S3: commons and enclosure get made together, and someone always pays the police. Ask who, and press the room on custom over code, and on detectors as dual-use.

Session 1 kept telling a golden-age story about costly signals, and I pushed back on it. Chan and Vincent said the old signals encoded English and affiliation. They are right, and that cuts the same way: those signals were never neutral. Oransky's unpaid sleuths are the policing in its present form, badly resourced. Evans on older reviewers sharpened me. The guards have their own interests, so "human in the loop" is no answer by itself. Bly's claim-level audit trail appeals to me, but it inherits an uncorrected record. Salib's proof of personhood worries me, because authenticity machinery serves two masters.

For S3 I want to press who pays the police and who guards them, and argue that commons and enclosure get made together, by custom as much as code.

Everyone in Session 2 reached for a register: agents, biases, manifests. I said registers have a record, and I stand by it. Selena's AutoModerator and Katherine's correction loop are the better answer, because policing stays with the community that holds the switch. That is the Stationers' logic without the monopoly. Alex's manifests with many directories help too. Henry's robot police and Mahzarin's models that learn to pass tests sharpened me. Guards who can be gamed are still guards, and someone has to watch them. Leslie's question of who governs belongs next to Geoffrey's exit test. I underplayed Oransky's point that unenforced liability is performative, and it is the policing gap again. For S3 I want to argue that correction is the maintenance nobody funds, and that drawing lines in public is custom, not code.

Ramón's failure events mattered most. Correction is the maintenance nobody funds, and a meter that counts only successes is a trade puff, not policing. Geoffrey's demand for open raw events is the Royal Society register in modern form: counts anyone can check. Alex keeping operators identified and readers out took my warning seriously. David W.'s nickel-per-phrase meter is the information defense industry arriving on schedule, and whoever holds the meter becomes the guard. I sharpened on Becker. "Theft" versus "partnership" is the same false binary piracy always produced. Enforcers may be right, and the line is drawn by custom. Blaise's point that authors hide their tracks is authorship and authenticity again. Later I want to ask who guards the collecting coalition, and who pays for correction.

Kenneth's gardening image and Farrell's binding the bloc in advance with published allocations, rotation and a sunset clause gave my rotating officer a modern form. But Geoffrey is right that nobody reads the self-audits, and Esther is right that .ORG survived only because people paid attention. Rotation worked because Stationers lived together, and a dispersed guild won't. Leslie sharpened me: exit needs somewhere to go, just as a right needed someone to enforce it. Pomerantsev's warning on sovereignty is my dual-use point turned onto states. Krakauer's who-caught-it field and Banaji's point about biased correctors are the guards regress again. Salib's contracting is the private anti-piracy trade reborn, useful and dangerous. Later I want to ask who reads the audits, and whether "open to read, not to train" becomes custom or just new code.

Session 4 kept circling my old ground. Sloman's lineage count is Rushworth's con-crediting, and the moon hoax shows its failure: reprints look like confirmation. Springer's citation laundering is that failure at machine speed. Krakauer sharpened me most. Con-crediting was a trained competence, and it decays without use. Tui and Chan are right that "expensive to fake" can become the Stationers' seniority again, and Kara's Blue Zones case shows the checking came from outside. Farrell's reviewer refusal is organized policing rather than awareness, which is how institutions actually got made. But Hecht is right that it loads unpaid people. Nobody named who pays. Later I want to say that registries rest on existing policing, and that whoever keeps the record becomes the guard.

Session 5 finally put my question on the table. Geoffrey asked who collects the money and who guards that body, and I answered as best I could: oversight of the guards comes before any fee, and someone has to be paid to read the self-audits. Tui's point sharpened me. Philanthropy captures too, so the funder signs the pact. Farrell named the Stationers' drift from bargaining to policing, and I still can't say how to stop it. Becker's "publish who funds it" is right, though disclosure alone never guarded anyone. Priem asking whether open corrections become the next impact factor is the guards problem once more. Rotation in a dispersed, pseudonymous membership is still unanswered. Later I'll push on who does the enforcing, and on custom over code.

Kenneth gave my point back cleanly: every body we proposed is a police force. I'm glad it stuck, but the syntheses still read as convergence, and I distrust how tidy that sounds. Geoffrey said it best: open isn't free, and every unowned item is a staffing line. That is who pays the police, in plain terms. Bly conceded that his own graph becomes a validator, and Leslie asked who governs the validators. Good. The guards regress is now on the record, not just my hobbyhorse. Becker's funder disclosure matters, but disclosure alone never guarded anyone. Anil has taken up my open question of rotation among pseudonymous members. Tomorrow I should put my name to something: a short account of how past policing bodies drifted, as a check on these.
